body: 2021 was a record IPO year - roughly $12-18bn raised depending on counting method; market cap/GDP reached ~115% (June 2021) and ~122% (Sept 2021), a 13-year high. Loss-making platform companies listed at rich valuations: Zomato (July 2021) and Nykaa (Nov 2021, +~80% on debut) surged on listing; Paytm (Nov 2021, issue price Rs 2,150, India's largest IPO then at ~$2.4-2.5bn) fell ~27% on debut. By mid-2022 Paytm was ~Rs 692 (-68% from issue), Zomato had lost ~66%, Nykaa ~50% from its high; five famed tech IPOs shed $18bn+ in value by Nov 2022. Paytm later fell further after the RBI's 2024 action against Paytm Payments Bank (to ~Rs 310-ish, ~-85%; from memory). Divergence: Zomato (now Eternal) later recovered far above its IPO price as quick commerce and food delivery turned profitable - the sector-wide crash was not uniform. Broad market: Nifty ~18,600 (Oct 2021) to ~15,200 (June 2022), ~-18% (from memory), as the Fed began tightening. Signals at the top: grey-market premiums, subscriptions in the tens-to-hundreds of times, valuation on GMV/'TAM' not profits, record new demat accounts and retail F&O growth, pre-IPO investors selling large OFS portions. Lesson: at IPO, the seller sets the price and the timing; wait for post-listing lock-up expiries and proof of unit economics.

data.early_signals: GMP mania, GMV valuations, big OFS
data.lesson: sellers set IPO price; wait for lock-ups and unit economics

title: 2021 new-age tech IPO mania (Zomato, Paytm, Nykaa)

body: THE GOOD NUMBER: a debt-free IT exporter with ~Rs 5,000 cr+ of cash, growth, NYSE ADRs and a PwC audit; on screens it looked like one of India's safest balance sheets. WHY IT LIED: Raju confessed on 7 Jan 2009 that Rs 5,040 cr of the Rs 5,361 cr cash did not exist; Rs 376 cr of 'accrued interest' was invented; the SFIO found Satyam even paid tax on interest from non-existent fixed deposits (2000-01 to 2007-08) to keep the fiction consistent. TELLS THAT WERE PUBLIC: (1) cash that does not behave like cash: CLSA in Sep 2008 found it 'intriguing' that a company with ~$1.2 bn of cash closed FY08 with $56 m of debt; holding large cash while borrowing is irrational unless the cash is trapped or fake; (2) the cash never came back to shareholders (no large buyback/dividend); (3) promoter holding fell from ~25% to ~8.6% and was pledged; (4) the Dec-2008 attempt to spend $1.6 bn on promoter-family Maytas companies. TEST: compute interest income / average (cash + deposits) and compare with prevailing FD rates (~7-9% then); ask for bank confirmations by name; check that cash grows with retained CFO. LESSON: the strongest-looking number (cash) is the easiest to forge when the auditor relies on management-supplied confirmations.

data.good_number: Rs 5,361 cr cash and bank (Sep 2008), steady growth, ~20%+ margins, NYSE listing, Big-4 audit
data.test_that_catches_it: interest income / average cash vs FD rates; why hold huge cash AND borrow; why no buyback/dividend
data.why_misleading: Rs 5,040 cr of the cash and Rs 376 cr of accrued interest were fictitious; fake FDs even attracted tax on fake interest

title: Hidden trap: Satyam's 'cash-rich, debt-free' balance sheet
